pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 9–11 years

- **Topic:** The Rock Cycle — rocks slowly change from one type to another over millions of years: igneous weathers into sediment, sediment compacts into sedimentary rock, heat and pressure make metamorphic rock, and melting starts the cycle again — a continuous process with no beginning or end.

- **Standards — UK (KS2→KS3 bridge):** In England the rock cycle and 'the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks' are DfE **KS3 Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere**. At KS2 the statutory groundwork is Y3 **Rocks** (compare/group rocks, fossils, soils) and Y4 weathering/erosion contexts. So this topic teaches KS3 content and should be framed as building on Y3 Rocks — note the placement honestly.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** The full rock cycle is **MS-ESS2-1** ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS2-1, MS-ESS2-4, MS-LS2-3]…'). The nearest elementary anchor is **4-ESS1-1** (evidence from rock layers/fossils for landscape change over time) and 4-ESS2 (weathering/erosion). This topic bridges into MS. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Prerequisites 'Types of Rock' and 'Earth's Layers'. The three types are already known; the NEW idea is that they INTERCONVERT via processes (weathering/erosion → deposition/compaction → heat & pressure → melting & cooling) and that the cycle is continuous — no start, no end, and NOT a fixed one-way sequence. The load-bearing insight is that a single rock can take many different PATHS around (and across) the cycle over deep time.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (early-formal, cyclic-systems + deep-time reasoning). Children can trace a loop but tend to memorise one fixed order and struggle with 'millions of years' and shortcut paths. Success = trace at least one complete path, name the process at each step, and state the cycle is continuous over vast time.
bestPractices: Teach it as PROCESSES connecting the three known types, not a new list — each arrow is an event (weathering, compaction, heat/pressure, melting, cooling).
Break the 'one fixed order' misconception by having children trace MULTIPLE valid paths, including shortcuts (e.g. any rock can be melted, or uplifted and weathered) so the cycle isn't a single loop.
Anchor the timescale explicitly — millions of years — and contrast with the human/quick events elsewhere in the domain so 'slow' is felt against 'fast'.
Use a concrete follow-one-grain narrative (a mineral grain journeys from a lava flow, to a beach, to a buried layer, to a squeezed metamorphic band, to melt) to make the abstract cycle a story.
Connect drivers to the rest of the domain: Earth's internal heat (melting), weathering/erosion at the surface, and burial/pressure — the cycle is powered by the same forces already met.
keyRepresentations: The classic rock-cycle diagram (three types as nodes; processes as labelled arrows, including cross-cutting shortcuts)
Follow-one-grain journey narrative around the cycle
Process cards: weathering/erosion, deposition/compaction, heat & pressure, melting, cooling/crystallising
A deep-time ribbon (millions of years) alongside the cycle to scale the pace
commonMisconceptions: The rock cycle is a fixed one-way sequence igneous→sedimentary→metamorphic (there are many paths and shortcuts; any type can become any other).
The cycle has a beginning and an end (it is continuous, with no start or finish).
Rocks change quickly / you could watch it happen (changes take thousands to millions of years).
Only volcanoes change rocks (surface weathering/erosion, burial pressure, and deep heat all drive the cycle).
Once a rock is metamorphic (or any type) it stays that way forever (it can be weathered, melted, or re-formed into another type).

learn.summary: For ages 9–11, teach the rock cycle as a set of PROCESSES connecting the three already-known rock types (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic), not as a new list to memorise. The load-bearing insight is that a single rock can take many different PATHS around and across the cycle — including shortcuts — over millions of years, with no fixed one-way order and no beginning or end. The strongest activity lets learners pick a rock, apply a process (weather/erode, deposit/compact, heat & pressure, melt, cool), watch it transform, and deliberately take different routes on repeat runs; a diagram and a consolidation task support naming, sequencing and reinforcement. Note: in England this is KS3 content building on Y3 Rocks; in the US it maps to NGSS MS-ESS2-1 with 4-ESS1-1 as the elementary anchor.

activities.title: Operate a rock-cycle machine: apply processes and change the path
feedback: When a learner only ever repeats igneous→sedimentary→metamorphic, prompt: 'Could you melt this sedimentary rock right now? What would it become?' to surface a shortcut.
When a learner takes a new route, affirm: 'You just skipped a step — a metamorphic rock went straight to sediment by weathering. That shows there's no fixed order.'

If a learner expects the change to be fast, point to the deep-time counter: 'Notice how much time the slow steps added, like weathering, burial and squeezing. A whole journey around the cycle usually takes millions of years, far longer than a lifetime, even though some steps, like lava cooling, can happen fast.'
If a learner thinks only volcanoes change rocks, highlight the weathering/erosion and burial/pressure actions: 'Surface weathering and burial change rocks too, not just melting.'
activities.rationale: A cycle of interconverting states with multiple paths is a system learners can drive; applying processes and watching transformations is intended to make the many-route, continuous nature experiential rather than a memorised diagram. Repeated runs with different routes target the 'fixed one-way order' misconception, and a per-step time counter anchors the deep-time scale. The source supports the taught model (continuous cycle with multiple pathways); the driveable-medium efficacy is an agent proposal, not source-established.
sourceClaims: The rock cycle is a continuous process with multiple pathways in which igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks interconvert via weathering/erosion, compaction, heat and pressure, and melting.
learnerActions: Pick a starting rock (e.g. a chunk of igneous rock).

Choose an action to apply: weather and erode it into sediment; bury and compact sediment into sedimentary rock; bake and squeeze a rock into metamorphic rock; or melt a rock and let it cool into igneous rock.

Watch the rock visibly transform with each action, and read the deep-time counter that adds time for each step. Most steps, like weathering, burial and metamorphism, take thousands to millions of years. Some, like lava cooling, can be quick, but a full journey usually takes millions of years.
Run the cycle again and deliberately take a DIFFERENT route — e.g. melt a sedimentary rock directly into igneous, or weather a metamorphic rock directly into sediment.
State out loud, after several runs, whether there is a fixed order or a finish line, and why.

Optionally switch to a 'follow one grain' story mode that narrates the long journey of the material in a single mineral grain (lava flow → beach sediment → buried layer → squeezed metamorphic band → melt, where the grain itself is destroyed and its material joins new magma).
activities.intendedInsight: The rock cycle is a continuous web of transformations: any rock type can become any other depending on which process acts, there are shortcuts, and the whole thing unfolds over millions of years with no start and no end.

activities.title: Rock-cycle diagram with reveal-on-arrow and shortcut flaps
feedback: If a learner names only the standard loop, ask them to find and trace one shortcut arrow and name its process.
Confirm correct naming: 'Yes — that arrow is weathering and erosion, turning rock into sediment.'
If a learner treats the diagram as a strict circle, draw attention to the shortcut flap so they see the extra paths.
activities.rationale: A labelled diagram is useful reference and supports naming the steps and timescales. A fixed diagram does not let learners drive transformations the way the operable machine can, so a learner may read it as a single loop; adding reveal-on-arrow and explicit shortcut highlighting keeps the many-paths idea visible. This supports, rather than replaces, hands-on tracing of multiple routes. Relative medium limits here are a proposal, not source-established.
learnerActions: Study a rock-cycle diagram showing the three types as nodes and processes as labelled arrows.
Tap or examine each arrow to reveal the process it represents and its approximate timescale.
Open an 'Is there only one way round?' prompt that highlights cross-cutting shortcut paths (e.g. melting from any type, uplift-and-weather from any type).
Drill into 'heat & pressure' to see how metamorphism forms.
Trace with a finger at least two different valid paths through the diagram and name the process at each step.
activities.intendedInsight: Each arrow in the cycle is a named event, and the diagram contains more than one legitimate route — including shortcuts — rather than a single loop.

activities.title: Consolidate: sequence, match and judge valid paths
feedback: For a correct shortcut choice: 'Right — a sedimentary rock can be melted and cool into igneous without passing through metamorphic first.'
For 'the cycle ends' answers: prompt 'What happens to a rock after it melts and cools? Could it change type again?' to reinstate the no-end idea.
For a mismatched process, pair it back: 'Compaction squeezes loose sediment together — which rock type does that make?'
activities.rationale: The processes and paths give clean, orderable and selectable structure: sequencing, matching and judging valid paths consolidate naming and reinforce that shortcuts are allowed. A recognition/selection task verifies and strengthens the model but does not by itself elicit a learner's independent construction of a full journey, so it works best after the operable and diagram activities.
learnerActions: Order a valid path around the cycle from a scrambled set of steps.
Match each process to the rock type it produces (e.g. heat & pressure without melting → metamorphic; compaction and cementation of sediment → sedimentary; cooling of molten rock → igneous).
Choose which of several offered paths is a valid rock-cycle path, including an option that uses a shortcut.
Answer whether the cycle has an end, and justify the answer in a sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can name processes, produce a correct sequence, recognise that shortcut paths are legitimate, and articulate that the cycle is continuous.

constraints: Prerequisites: learners should already know the three rock types ('Types of Rock') and Earth's layers; the NEW idea here is that the types interconvert via processes and that the cycle is continuous.

Frame placement honestly: this is KS3 content (DfE KS3 Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere) built on Y3 Rocks in England; in the US it bridges toward NGSS MS-ESS2-1, with 4-ESS1-1 (rock-record change over time) and 4-ESS2 (weathering/erosion) as the nearest elementary anchors.
Teach arrows as events (weathering/erosion, deposition/compaction, heat & pressure, melting, cooling/crystallising), not as a new vocabulary list.
Deliberately require multiple paths and shortcuts so learners do not fossilise a single igneous→sedimentary→metamorphic order.
Anchor the timescale explicitly in millions of years; contrast with faster surface events so 'slow' is felt against 'fast'.
The diagram activity is a reference scaffold: a fixed diagram can still teach naming and routes, but it does not let learners drive transformations, so pair it with hands-on path-tracing.

The sequence/match/judge tasks are recognition-and-ordering responses; they consolidate and check but do not by themselves elicit a learner's independent construction of a full journey — use the operable machine or an explanation prompt for that.

Success criteria: trace at least one complete path, name the process at each step, and state that the cycle is continuous over vast time; stronger success is explaining that any type can become any other via different paths and shortcuts.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three cited sources are marked verified:false in the row (NGSS mapping and the USGS/BGS rock-cycle description); the DfE curriculum citation is verified:true. Treat standards mappings and the continuous-multiple-pathways description as legacy, unverified claims.

sourceClaims were scoped to where the source directly backs the claim: the USGS/BGS continuous-multiple-pathways description underpins activity 1's taught model, but it does not establish the pedagogical efficacy of a diagram or a consolidation/selection task, so those carry []. Activity 1's source citation supports only the factual model it teaches, not the driveable-medium efficacy. No source attests medium superiority or activity effectiveness.

The legacy row's 'poor fit' entries claimed a 3D environment 'adds no relevant insight' and a conversation has 'no in-role persona central'. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws; omitted as boilerplate rather than asserted as limits. A 3D or dialogue treatment is not inherently valueless, but no distinct activity was specified for them here.

The legacy claim that a static image 'tends to reinforce a single fixed loop' is a relative tendency, not an absolute limit; softened to note a fixed diagram does not let learners drive transformations while still teaching naming and routes.

Checked for internal consistency: the transformations (weathering→sediment, compaction→sedimentary, heat & pressure→metamorphic, melting+cooling→igneous) and the shortcut examples (metamorphic→sediment; sedimentary→melt→igneous) are coherent with the stated continuous-cycle model; no arithmetic or force/motion claims present to audit.

The assessment's diagnostic (friend draws a single fixed circle) and probe questions were preserved in spirit as feedback prompts; the fixed-circle misconception is treated as the error to correct, never offered as a valid learner answer. Assessment fields themselves were not modified.

probeDeeper: Can a metamorphic rock turn straight into sediment without becoming igneous first? How?
What process would turn a sedimentary rock into an igneous one?
Roughly how long does it take a rock to change type — years, or much longer?
Is there a 'first' rock or a 'start' to the cycle? Why or why not?
assess.correctAnswer: No — it isn't a fixed one-way loop. A rock can take many different paths and shortcuts: any type can become any other. For example, a metamorphic rock can be weathered straight into sediment (skipping 'back to igneous'), or a sedimentary rock can be melted and cool into igneous. Weathering, pressure, heat and melting can act in different orders, all over millions of years.

errorPatterns.pattern: The rock cycle is a fixed one-way circle — always igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → igneous in that order
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show multiple pathways — metamorphic weathering to sediment, or sedimentary melting to igneous.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — it's a fixed circle that always goes in that one order.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Insists on one strict sequence; denies shortcuts.

errorPatterns.pattern: Rocks change quickly — you could watch a rock go round the cycle
errorPatterns.nextMove: Emphasise deep time; the processes are extremely slow.
errorPatterns.distractor: The cycle happens quickly — a rock goes round in a short time.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: No sense of the millions-of-years timescale.

errorPatterns.pattern: A rock can only move 'forwards', never skip or reverse a step
errorPatterns.nextMove: Any type can turn into any other depending on which process acts.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies e.g. metamorphic turning directly into sediment.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the rock cycle as a fixed one-way circle, or thinks rocks change quickly.
responseLevels.full: Explains any rock type can become any other by different paths and shortcuts (e.g. metamorphic→sediment, sedimentary→melt→igneous), driven by weathering/pressure/heat/melting over millions of years — a web, not a single loop.
responseLevels.partial: Names the types and processes and can trace the standard loop but insists the order is fixed / denies shortcuts.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A friend draws the rock cycle as a single circle: igneous always turns into sedimentary, then always into metamorphic, then back to igneous — always in that one order. Is the rock cycle really a fixed one-way loop like that? Explain what can actually happen to a rock.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can recite the three types and a circle diagram yet believe the order is fixed. Asking whether it's really a one-way loop forces the many-paths insight; a child holding the single-loop model insists on the strict sequence.
